newsitem.title: UK: UK ad industry sees wider issue in tobacco ad ban.
newsitem.headline: UK ad industry sees wider issue in tobacco ad ban.

text.p: Britain's advertising industry expects the newly elected Labour government to act quickly on its promise to ban tobacco advertising, but it is more concerned about a precedent being set for the regulation of other kinds of advertising.
"I suspect the game is up on tobacco advertising," Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director general of Britain's Advertising Association (AA), told Reuters.
Stanbrook expects a tobacco ad ban could take effect early in 1998.

Said Philip Circus, legal affairs director for the Institute of Practioners in Advertising (IPA), a trade group representing ad agencies: "I think cigarette advertising could be illegal in this country by Christmas."

The tobacco industry, itself, is resigned to an ad ban. "We obviously hope they don't do anything, but we're realistic enough to know that they have made a commitment in their manifesto, and as far as we know they intend to keep it," John Carlisle, executive director for industry affairs for Britain's Tobacco Manufacturers' Association, told Reuters.

A Labour Party spokesman said it was too early to forecast when a tobacco ad ban might be implemented. But he emphasised the party's seriousness. "It's a manifesto commitment to ban tobacco advertising," he said.

The tobacco industry, already banned from advertising on television and radio in the UK, spends about 53 million pounds ($86.7 million) a year to advertise its products on billboards and in newspapers in Britain.
Advertising industry officials said a tobacco ad ban would infringe on the freedom of commercial speech.
"Once you set a precedent, the enemies of advertising in other sectors -- like alcohol, toys, food and confectionery -- will see that as something to aim for," said Circus.
"We're not fighting for the tobacco industry," he added. "We're fighting for the freedom of commercial speech."

The AA's Stanbrook noted that many officials in other industries, such as alcoholic beverages and confectionery, are not happy with a defense of tobacco advertising. "But we're convinced that with the fall of tobacco other things will be next in line," he said.
The defense of tobacco advertising, however, has not been unanimously popular.
"We've been criticised within the industry for our strong defense of the right to advertise and probably lost quite a few friends," Stanbrook said.

The issue has also been controversial within the IPA. "It is difficult for us as an organisation," Circus said. "The vast majority of our members believe in defending freedom on commercial speech. Is there a contrary view? Yes."
"But we have to take a broad view," Circus added. "Tobacco advertising is worth quite a lot of money to a lot of our key members."
By contrast, other members refuse to accept any tobacco advertising.
Not everyone in the ad industry believes a tobacco ad ban would be the first step toward other advertising restrictions.
"The expected ban on tobacco advertising is almost a red herring," said Richard Pinder, deputy managing director of Ogilvy & Mather, London.
Pinder acknowledged that a tobacco ad ban could open the door to other restrictions, but said the Labour Party has given no sign it would go down that road.
"They've got an intelligent approach to advertising and marketing and to taxation," he said.
In addition, he downplayed the monetary impact, as did the AA's Stanbrook.
Even if the 50 million pounds spent annually on tobacco advertising in the UK were allocated to a single large agency, its loss would be a major but not a crippling blow, Pinder said.
In contrast to the tobacco advertising spend in Britian, UK commercial radio generates 400 million pounds in ad revenues each year -- and that is dwarfed by television ad spends.
The one remaining issue is whether the Labour government will rely on legislation or a voluntary agreement to implement a tobacco ad ban.
The existing ban on television and radio advertising of tobacco and restrictions on how tobacco is advertised in other media is defined in a voluntary agreement with the tobacco industry.
Carlisle, of the Tobacco Manufacturers' Association, said the industry prefers voluntary agreements.
A voluntary agreement could give the industry room to negotiate the continued existence of sports sponsorship deals -- an area in which the Labour Party has already indicated a willingness to talk.
"We're happy to discuss whatever they put before us," Carlisle said. "Whether it's advertising or sponsorship, we would like to have meaningful discussion."
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
